title: Shopping, numbers 11-100 and money
description: Count to a hundred and beyond, ask prices, bargain and pay.

guide.title: Eleven to nineteen
guide.text:
The teens are built on hattu (ten), which shrinks to han- or hadi- in front of the unit:

11 hannondu, 12 hanneradu, 13 hadimooru, 14 hadinaalku, 15 hadinaidu, 16 hadinaaru, 17 ಹದಿನೇಳು (hadinelu, long e), 18 ಹದಿನೆಂಟು (hadinentu), 19 ಹತ್ತೊಂಬತ್ತು (hattombattu).

Notice that 19 keeps the full hattu: hattu + ombattu.

guide.title: The tens
guide.text:
The tens end in -vattu or -pattu (a worn-down hattu):

20 ippattu, 30 moovattu, 40 nalavattu, 50 aivattu, 60 aravattu, 70 eppattu, 80 ಎಂಬತ್ತು (embattu), 90 ತೊಂಬತ್ತು (tombattu), 100 ನೂರು (nooru).

Take care with the similar-sounding pairs: eppattu (70) and embattu (80); ombattu (9) and tombattu (90).

1,000 is ಸಾವಿರ (saavira); 100,000 is ಲಕ್ಷ (laksha), the 'lakh' used all over India; ten million is ಕೋಟಿ (koti), a 'crore'.

guide.title: Putting numbers together
guide.text:
Tens and units join into one word, ten first, and the final u of the ten drops before a vowel (sandhi again): ippattu + ondu = ippattondu (21); ippattu + aidu = ippattaidu (25); moovattu + aaru = moovattaaru (36); nalavattu + eradu = nalavatteradu (42). Before a consonant the u becomes a: ಇಪ್ಪತ್ತಮೂರು (ippattamooru) 23, ಇಪ್ಪತ್ತನಾಲ್ಕು (ippattanaalku) 24; in fast speech that a is swallowed: ippatmooru, ippatnaalku.

Hundreds: 100 nooru, 200 ಇನ್ನೂರು (innooru), 300 ಮುನ್ನೂರು (munnooru), 400 ನಾನೂರು (naanooru), 500 ಐನೂರು (ainooru), then aarunooru, elunooru, entunooru, ombainooru. A hundred plus something is noora ...: ನೂರ ಐವತ್ತು (noora aivattu) 150, usually run together as nooraivattu.

Thousands: eradu saavira (2,000), hattu saavira (10,000).

guide.title: Prices and bargaining
guide.text:
The rupee is ರೂಪಾಯಿ (roopaayi). The noun stays singular after a number: nooru roopaayi, 'a hundred rupees'.

To ask a price: idara bele eshtu? ('what is the price of this?') or simply ಇದು ಎಷ್ಟು? (idu eshtu?), 'how much is this?'. For produce sold by weight: keji eshtu? 'how much a kilo?'.

'For a hundred rupees' uses the dative: nooru roopaayige kodi, 'give it for a hundred'.

Bargaining words: ದುಬಾರಿ (dubaari) expensive; ಜಾಸ್ತಿ (jaasti) too much; ಕಡಿಮೆ ಮಾಡಿ (kadime maadi) reduce it; ಕೊನೆ ಬೆಲೆ (kone bele) last price. In markets and with street vendors bargaining is expected; in shops with fixed prices it is not.

ಒಟ್ಟು (ottu) is 'total'; ಚಿಲ್ಲರೆ (chillare) is 'small change'.

examples.english: Please reduce the price a little.
Give it for a hundred rupees.

guide.title: Halves, quarters and weights
guide.text:
ಅರ್ಧ (ardha) is 'half': ardha keji, 'half a kilo'. ಕಾಲು (kaalu) is 'a quarter' (and also 'leg'); ಮುಕ್ಕಾಲು (mukkaalu) is 'three quarters'.

'And a half' is -ವರೆ (-vare) joined to the number, whose final u lengthens to oo: ಒಂದೂವರೆ (ondoovare) one and a half; ಎರಡೂವರೆ (eradoovare) two and a half; mooroovare, three and a half.

Weights and measures use the English words: ಕೆಜಿ (keji) kilo; ಗ್ರಾಂ (graam) gram; ಲೀಟರ್ (leetar) litre. A dozen is ಡಜನ್ (dajan) - bananas are sold by the dozen.

phrases.note: In shops people often just say 'idu eshtu?' (ಇದು ಎಷ್ಟು?).

phrases.english: Please reduce the price a little.

phrases.note: 'nanage ... beku' = 'I want / need ...'. The e in beku is long.

phrases.english: Do you have a bigger size?

phrases.note: Literally 'Do you take cards?' (spoken form). Written: tegedukollutteeraa? (ತೆಗೆದುಕೊಳ್ಳುತ್ತೀರಾ?)
In Bengaluru shops a carry bag is often called 'kavar' (ಕವರ್).
summane = just, for no particular reason.

phrases.english: Give it for a hundred rupees.
Half a kilo of tomatoes, please.
